name: Dr Geoffrey Omuse; Why I chose to be a Clinical Pathologist

content.title: Dr Geoffrey Omuse; Why I chose to be a Clinical Pathologist
content.summary: The main role of a clinical pathologist is to support the diagnosis of disease by using laboratory examination to test blood, body fluids, tissues and cells.

content.text: Clinical pathology also commonly referred to as laboratory medicine is a branch of pathology with several sub-specialities, which includes blood bank and transfusion medicine, haematopathology, clinical microbiology, clinical chemistry, molecular pathology and immunology.

The main role of a clinical pathologist is to support the diagnosis of disease by using laboratory examination to test blood, body fluids, tissues and cells. Clinical pathology is indeed a critical component of patient management as it has been estimated that up to 70% of all patient management decisions in developed countries are dependent upon a pathology examination.
In essence, our work as pathologists involves preventing, diagnosing, treating and monitoring diseases to ensure that people stay as healthy as possible.

Personally, I decided to pursue a career in clinical pathology after realizing that my practice as a medical doctor is determined by the kind of laboratory support that is available in any particular hospital.

In the district hospital where I previously worked, we had rudimentary laboratory facilities, which limited the extent to which I could properly examine a patient. Many times, I would end up treating most patients who developed fever, headache and joint pains for either malaria, typhoid or brucellosis.

When I joined the Aga Khan University (AKU) Medical College, Department of Pathology to pursue a master's degree in clinical pathology, I was impressed by the wide array of laboratory equipment's at my disposal.

This inspired me to carry out a small study on the accuracy of one of the tests frequently used in district hospitals to diagnose typhoid fever called widal test. The widal test was developed over a century ago and remains one of the world's most widely used diagnostic tests but suffers from significant limitations in its reliability.

The gold standard for diagnosing typhoid fever is growing the bacteria from a blood or bone marrow sample. This was not available where I used to work and is not available in most hospitals in Kenya. Fortunately, blood and bone marrow cultures had been routinely done at Aga Khan University Hospital Nairobi (AKUHN) for several years and I was able to use archived data to determine the sensitivity of the widal test in diagnosing typhoid fever.

To my surprise, the widal test only had a sensitivity of 26% meaning that out of 100 people with typhoid fever, the test would only identify 26 people. Given that typhoid fever can result in severe illness and even cause death, these findings helped inform the hospital's decision to discourage clinicians from using the widal test and instead, encouraged the use of blood and bone marrow cultures to detect patients with typhoid fever.

Currently, there are only about 100 pathologists practising in the various fields of pathology in the country. With the current population of Kenya standing at 47.6 million, according to the 2019 Kenya National Bureau of Statistics data, this means that we have one pathologist serving around 500,000 Kenyans, which translates to 0.2 per 100,000 Kenyans. In comparison, in 2010, the United States had approximately 18,000 practicing pathologists which is equivalent to 5.7 per 100 000 population.

As the Chair of the Kenya Association of Clinical Pathologists (KACP), I am fortunate to have the opportunity to not only practice as a clinical pathologist at a world class laboratory at AKUHN but also I'm involved in generating new knowledge through research as well as educating the next generation of clinical pathologists.

Furthermore, I am playing my role in building a critical and knowledgeable workforce of pathologists that is necessary in advancing the governments agenda of achieving universal healthcare in the country.

Dr Geoffrey Omuse is an Assistant Professor and Consultant Clinical Pathologist, Department of Pathology, Aga Khan University Hospital Nairobi. He is also a Fellow College of Pathologists East, Central and Southern Africa (FCPathECSA)
